factor: Publishers’ lack of control over AI content presentation
Deployment of AI with intention to harm, mislead, or troll
AI cited to justify job cuts
Lack of internal transparency about AI-related management decisions
Lack of internal standards regarding AI use

Process/Governance Failures: Publishers’ lack of control over AI content presentation
Intentional Misuse: Deployment of AI with intention to harm, mislead, or troll
Labor/organizational decisions: AI cited to justify job cuts
Lack of internal transparency about AI-related management decisions
Lack of internal standards regarding AI use

systems_definitions.Chatbot (general use):
Open-ended, general-purpose use of a conversational AI system where no more specific task code applies (e.g., a user asking an AI open-ended questions about the news) 

**Do not use when the chatbot is performing a task covered by another code – code the SPECIFIC task instead.**
systems_definitions.News summarization:
Use of AI to produce condensed versions or summaries of news content, without materially changing its claims or substance.

**The transformation of content into a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT version/format should be coded as 'Remixing/repurposing'**
systems_definitions.Text generation:
Use of AI to assist in producing materially new text that had not been previously reported/published (e.g., generating an article or story from scratch or from source material or notes). 

**The summarization of EXISTING news content should be coded as 'News summarization'; the use of AI to EDIT already-written text should be coded as ‘Editing’; the transformation of existing news content INTO ANOTHER FORMAT should be coded as 'Remixing/repurposing’**
systems_definitions.Remixing/repurposing:
Use of AI to transform existing news content into a materially different version or format (e.g., turning a text-based article into a video or podcast) where the underlying reporting or content is substantially preserved rather than newly generated. 

**Condensing or summarization of news content WITHOUT transforming it into a materially different version should be coded as 'News summarization'; Use of AI to produce MATERIALLY NEW content should be coded as 'Text generation'**
systems_definitions.Editing: Use of AI to process already-written text without materially changing its content (e.g. copyediting, proofreading, light rewriting for clarity/style)
systems_definitions.Deepfake generation:
Use of AI to generate a digital image, video, or audio that falsely depicts a specific real person, place or event doing, saying, or showing something that did not actually happen. 

**AI-generated multimedia content which depicts people, places, or events that DO NOT EXIST should be coded as 'Synthetic multimedia generation'**
systems_definitions.Synthetic video/image generation:
Use of AI to generate video, image, or audio content depicting people, places, or events that do not exist or did not actually occur, without reference to or manipulation of any specific real person, place, or event (as opposed to deepfakes, which depict a specific real referent)

**AI-generated multimedia content which depicts REAL people, places or events should be coded as 'Deepfake generation'**
systems_definitions.Translation: Use of AI to translate text, audio, or video from one language to another.
systems_definitions.Other: (Use when none of the above system codes apply. Record the specific system type in the notes field.)

developers_definitions.In-house AI system:
The AI system’s core capability was developed internally by the journalism entity involved in the incident, built from the ground up rather than adapted from an external model.

**Systems that contain any foundational or core model component that originated externally - even if fine-tuned, customized or heavily configured in-house – should be coded as ‘Hybrid/in-house tool on vendor model’**
developers_definitions.AI vendor:
The AI system’s core capability was developed by an external company or organization, rather than the journalism entity involved, and is used substantially as delivered – including informal or unauthorized use.

**If a journalism entity built or customized a distinct tool around an externally developed core model/API, code as ‘Hybrid/in-house tool on vendor model**
developers_definitions.Hybrid/in-house tool on vendor model: A tool was built or customized by the journalism entity involved, but its core underlying AI capability (e.g. foundation model, API) was developed by an external vendor.
developers_definitions.Unknown/unspecified: Whether the AI system was developed in-house or by an external vendor cannot be determined from available documentation

actor_definitions.News organization/publisher: Professional media outlet or publisher, including editorial staff and management, whose action, decision, or failure caused or contributed to the (alleged) harm.
actor_definitions.Individual journalist: A journalist or media worker (e.g., staff, freelance, or independent worker) whose own action or decision, made independently of institutional process or sanction, caused or contributed to the (alleged) harm.
actor_definitions.AI developer:
A company or entity that built or provided the AI system or AI-powered feature that was involved in the (alleged) harm.  

**Use this code when the incident implicates a company’s identifiable AI product or feature; otherwise, a company whose NON-AI products/features were involved in the (alleged) harm should be coded as 'Tech platform'**
actor_definitions.Tech platform:
A technology company (e.g., search engine, social media platform, or content distributor) whose non-AI feature or product was involved in the (alleged) harm. 

**Use this code when the incident implicates a general platform mechanism not specifically branded or identifiable as an AI product; a company whose AI-SPECIFIC products/features were involved in the (alleged) harm should be coded as 'AI developer'**
actor_definitions.Content farm/SEO-manipulation actor: An entity that generates a large amount of web content – typically by republishing, remixing or repackaging existing news content, often without authorization from the original publisher – for the purpose of exploiting search or platform recommendation systems for traffic or advertising revenue.
actor_definitions.Mis/disinformation actor: An entity whose primary identifiable intention is producing or spreading false or misleading content – distinct from an entity that produces misleading content as a side effect of another primary purpose.
actor_definitions.PR/marketing agency: Agency or firm producing or distributing content on behalf of a client.
actor_definitions.Unknown/unspecified: The identity or type of actor cannot be determined from the available documentation.

factor_definitions.Inadequate human oversight: Could be reasonably inferred when outputs indicate human-in-the-loop protocols appear to have been absent, minimal, or not followed when reviewing an AI-generated output before publication or deployment. This includes cases where an AI system was reasonably suited to the task but its output was published without adequate human review and contained errors.
factor_definitions.Contextually inappropriate application o: Could be reasonably inferred when AI tools were applied to tasks, formats, or subject matter for which they were ill-suited or untested, such as sensitive, breaking, or highly nuanced news topics. There was a mismatch between the task and the tool's capabilities, regardless of whether human review was in place.
factor_definitions.Lack of audience disclosure:
AI-generated or AI-assisted content was published without clear labeling, attribution, or disclosure to audiences. 

**Instances where STAFF (rather than audiences) were not informed about AI use should be coded as 'Lack of internal transparency about AI-related management decisions'**
factor_definitions.Publishers’ lack of control over AI cont: A publisher's content was surfaced, summarized, or presented in an AI output (e.g., a search engine's AI summary) in a manner the publisher did not authorize or control.
factor_definitions.Publisher’s lack of due diligence: A publisher failed to verify sources, credentials, or accuracy before commissioning or publication, (e.g., failing to confirm that a freelancer is a real person or failing to verify underlying claims or pitches).
factor_definitions.Inadequate content moderation by platfor: A platform hosting or distributing AI-generated or AI-related content failed to detect, flag, or remove harmful or fraudulent material.
factor_definitions.Deployment of AI with intention to harm,: AI was intentionally used to deceive, manipulate, or harm audiences, sources or institutions (in a manner not captured by a more specific intentional misuse category)
factor_definitions.AI-based hoaxing/counterfeiting of journ:
AI was used to replicate a specific journalist's voice, writing style, image, or persona (e.g., via deepfaked content or stylistic text generation) without informed consent, or AI-generated content was falsely attributed to real journalists or news organizations.

**AI-generated content which is attributed to journalists/organizations that DO NOT EXIST should be coded as 'AI-based hoaxing/counterfeiting of journalists/outlets'**
factor_definitions.AI-based mimicry of established journali:
AI was used to replicate a specific journalist's voice, writing style, image, or persona (e.g., via deepfaked content or stylistic text generation) without informed consent, or AI-generated content was falsely attributed to real journalists or news organizations.

**AI-generated content which is attributed to journalists/organizations that DO NOT EXIST should be coded as 'AI-based hoaxing/counterfeiting of journalists/outlets'**
factor_definitions.SEO gaming:
AI-generated content was used to artificially manipulate search engine rankings or platform recommendation systems (e.g, backlinking schemes) 

**The use of AI to specifically aid in the EXPLOITATION OF LAPSED DOMAINS should be coded as 'Expired domain abuse'**
factor_definitions.Expired domain abuse:
A lapsed or expired domain, often previously belonging to a legitimate publisher, was acquired and repurposed to host AI-generated content while exploiting the domain's residual search ranking or backlink authority.

**More general use of AI to artificially manipulate search rankings, which DOES NOT INVOLVE EXPLOITING LAPSED DOMAINS, should be coded as 'SEO gaming'**
factor_definitions.AI substitution for human journalists: An organization used AI to functionally replace journalists in tasks they would typically perform (e.g., reporting, writing, or editorial review).
factor_definitions.AI cited to justify job cuts: An organization cited the adoption or capabilities of AI tools as a rhetorical or strategic justification for layoffs, role eliminations, or restructuring of journalistic staff, regardless of whether AI was the substantive cause.
factor_definitions.Lack of internal transparency about AI-r:
Rank-and-file staff were excluded from or not informed about organizational decisions regarding AI deployment.

**Not disclosing AI use to AUDIENCES should be coded as 'Lack of audience disclosure'.**
factor_definitions.Lack of internal standards regarding AI: Absence of internal policies or guidelines governing AI use. (Code only when the absence of such standards is explicitly documented.)

harm_definitions.Publication of low-effort AI outputs/slo:
Low-effort, low-value or filler AI-generated content was published with minimal human refinement.

**The publication of AI-generated content that is MISLEADING OR INACCURATE should be coded as ‘Publication of erroneous AI outputs’**
harm_definitions.Publication of erroneous AI outputs:
AI-generated errors introduced during the AI generation process were published.

**The publication of AI-generated content that is not necessarily inaccurate but LACKS IN QUALITY should be coded as ‘Publication of low-effort AI outputs/slop’. The regurgitation of errors via AI outputs should be coded as ‘Amplification of misinformation’ or ‘Propaganda/disinformation’, depending on the intent of the actor who produced that information**
harm_definitions.Plagiarism:
AI-generated content reproduced others' work without correct attribution.

**An AI-generated output attributing a claim to a NONEXISTENT source should be coded as 'Citation fabrication'; An AI-generated output that cites a real source but MISREPRESENTS its contents should be coded as 'Distorted source representation'**
harm_definitions.Citation fabrication:
AI-generated content cited sources that do not exist, or attributed claims or quotations to sources that did not actually contain them.

**An AI-generated output cites a real source but MISREPRESENTS its contents should be coded as 'Distorted source representation'; An AI-generated output that reproduces others' work WITHOUT ATTRIBUTION should be coded as 'Plagiarism’**
harm_definitions.Distorted source representation:
AI-generated content mischaracterized, distorted, or misrepresented the substance of a real, correctly cited source, such as through inaccurate summarization.

**An AI-generated output attributing a claim to a NONEXISTENT source should be coded as 'Citation fabrication'; An AI-generated output that reproduces others' work WITHOUT ATTRIBUTION should be coded as 'Plagiarism'**
harm_definitions.Amplification of misinformation:
AI tools spread or scale false/misleading claims.

**The spread of inaccurate information for which there is EVIDENCE OF MOTIVATION to advance a political or ideological agenda should be coded as 'Propaganda/disinformation'; the spread of inaccurate information introduced during the AI generation process should be coded as ‘Publication of erroneous AI outputs‘**
harm_definitions.Propaganda/disinformation:
AI was used to generate or scale persuasive or inaccurate content serving a political or ideological agenda, distinguished from misinformation by intent. 

**The spread of inaccurate information in instances where there is NO EVIDENCE OF MOTIVATION to advance a political or ideological agenda should be coded as 'Amplification of misinformation'; the spread of inaccurate information introduced during the AI generation process should be coded as ‘Publication of erroneous AI outputs‘**
harm_definitions.Exposure to offensive content: Party/ies exposed to the content claimed they found it upsetting or problematic.
harm_definitions.Collateral professional harm:
Individual journalists or organizations experienced or alleged damage to their reputations or credibility as a result of an action in which they did not directly partake.

**Consequences that resulted from actions DIRECTLY taken by journalists/organizations should be coded as 'Direct professional harm'**
harm_definitions.Direct professional harm:
Individual journalists or organizations experienced or alleged damage to their reputations or credibility as a result of an action in which they directly partook.

**Consequences that resulted from actions NOT DIRECTLY taken by journalists/organizations should be coded as 'Collateral professional harm'**
harm_definitions.Undermining of journalistic standards: A journalist or organization experienced or alleged erosion of professional norms (e.g., verification, sourcing, editorial review) as a result of AI use.
harm_definitions.Journalists being duped: A journalist or news organization was misled by AI-generated or AI-amplified content (e.g., unknowingly relying on or reporting fabricated AI output as fact).
harm_definitions.Breach of contract: Violation of established AI policies, labor contracts, or codes of conduct.
harm_definitions.Displacement of human judgement:
Editorial discretion was ceded to AI even where the relevant jobs or roles remained in place.

**COMPLETE ELIMINATION of jobs/roles previously performed by humans should be coded as 'Displacement of human labor.'**
harm_definitions.Displacement of human labor:
Jobs or roles were eliminated or reduced as a result of AI adoption.

**The deployment of AI to complete tasks that were previously performed by a human, SHORT OF COMPLETE ELIMINATION of jobs, should be coded as 'Displacement of human judgement'**
harm_definitions.Increased workload / burden on journalis: AI-related tasks (e.g., correcting AI errors, verifying AI outputs, managing AI tools) imposed additional labor on journalists beyond their typical workload.
harm_definitions.Economic harm to publisher(s)/journalist: Revenue or business harm (allegedly) resulted from AI-related activity (e.g., budget cuts or legal fees).
harm_definitions.Litigation burden:
A qualifying incident resulted in legal costs, liability exposure, or regulatory or compliance consequences for an involved party. 

**This does not apply when the central harm is a copyright or licensing dispute itself -- see Exclusion Criterion 5.**
harm_definitions.Disintermediation: Relationship between publisher and audience was disrupted (e.g., audience consuming AI-summarized news without visiting the original source).
harm_definitions.Perpetuation of stereotypes: AI-generated content reproduced or reinforced harmful stereotypes (e.g. racial, gender, ethnic or religious) about a group in its output.
harm_definitions.Misrepresentation of individuals depicte: AI outputs misquoted or misrepresented interview subjects, sources or other individuals depicted in content.
harm_definitions.Dignity harm to individuals depicted: Specific, identified Individuals depicted in AI-generated content (as opposed to groups in general) were subjected to racist, discriminatory or degrading portrayals.
harm_definitions.Loss of diversity: AI use contributed to a loss of diversity of viewpoints in published content.
harm_definitions.Privacy harm: An individual’s personal data or likeness was exposed or used without consent through AI training or outputs (e.g., deepfaked individuals). Distinct from harms specific to journalists’ professional identity, since this can apply to non-journalist subjects
harm_definitions.Scams: AI was used to defraud audiences.

harmed_party_definitions.Self:
The inciting actor was (allegedly) harmed by the outcomes of their own deployment or decision. 

**Code this in addition to, not instead of, the specific party-type code that matches the inciting actor – ‘Self’ flags that the harmed party and inciting actor are the same entity, not a separate category of the harmed party.**
harmed_party_definitions.Journalist(s): Individual journalists or media workers were (allegedly) harmed (e.g. reputational damage, job loss, misattributed work).
harmed_party_definitions.News organization/publisher: A news organization or publisher, as a collective entity distinct from its individual staff, was (allegedly) harmed (e.g., reputational or financial harm to the organization itself).
harmed_party_definitions.Sources/subjects of coverage: Individuals, experts, or groups referenced, quoted, depicted, or interviewed within the content were (allegedly) harmed.
harmed_party_definitions.Audience/readers: People who consumed the content as readers or viewers of the news organization involved were (allegedly) harmed (e.g., exposed to misinformation, deceived, defrauded).
harmed_party_definitions.General public: People were (allegedly) harmed more diffusely, independent of direct readership of the specific outlet involved (e.g., broader erosion of public trust in news, exposure to AI-generated misinformation via other channels).
